title: Forgiveness, Ten Lepers, and the Coming Kingdom
summary: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble, commands repeated forgiveness, and tells his apostles that even small faith is enough and that servants do not earn thanks for doing their duty. On the road he heals ten men with leprosy, and only one, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks. Asked when the kingdom will come, he says it is already in their midst, then warns his disciples that the day of the Son of Man will arrive suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot.
story: Jesus is still traveling toward Jerusalem, and Luke reminds us of it in verse 11. After the hard sayings about money in chapter 16, the teaching turns to life inside the community of disciples: how they treat the weak, how they forgive, how they think of their own service. The healing of the lepers then shows who actually responds to Jesus with gratitude, an outsider, echoing the Samaritan of chapter 10. The chapter ends by looking forward. The kingdom is present in Jesus now, but its full arrival, the day of the Son of Man, is still to come, and the disciples must not be caught unready. That two-sided view of the kingdom, already here and not yet complete, runs through the rest of Luke.
historical:
Luke says Jesus was passing between Samaria and Galilee, the border region where the Jewish territory of Galilee met Samaria to its south. Samaritans lived in the central hill country around Mount Gerizim. They traced their descent from the northern tribes of Israel, accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture, and worshiped at Gerizim rather than Jerusalem. Jews regarded them as a mixed and heretical people, and the hostility ran both ways. In this story a Samaritan is found among Jewish sufferers, since shared disease and exclusion could erase the usual boundaries.

The Law of Moses (Leviticus 13 and 14) gave priests the task of inspecting skin diseases, declaring a person unclean, and later confirming healing so that the person could return to worship and community. The Hebrew and Greek words translated leprosy covered a range of skin conditions, not only the disease now called Hansen's disease. Those afflicted had to live apart and call out a warning when others came near, which is why the ten stood at a distance and shouted. By sending them to the priests before they were healed, Jesus asked them to act on his word.
cultural:
Servants and slaves were ordinary members of households in the Roman world, and Jesus' picture in verses 7 to 10 assumes the social expectations of his hearers: a master did not wait on the worker who came in from the field. Jesus uses that shared assumption, not to endorse slavery, but to show disciples that obedience to God is owed, not a favor that puts God in their debt. Millstones were heavy stones used to grind grain; a large one was turned by a donkey. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, and the mulberry tree (probably the black mulberry) was known for deep, spreading roots, which makes the picture of uprooting it by a word all the more extreme.

The examples of Noah and Lot drew on Genesis 6 to 7 and 19, stories every Jewish hearer knew. The point is not that eating, marrying, or building are wrong, but that ordinary life absorbed people so fully that they did not see judgment coming. Grinding grain was daily women's work, often done in pairs at a hand mill. Flat roofs served as living space, and houses had outside stairs, so someone on the roof could flee without going back inside.
literary: The chapter gathers several short units. Verses 1 to 10 are a cluster of sayings to the disciples on stumbling, forgiveness, faith, and duty, joined by the theme of life in the community. Verses 11 to 19 are a healing story with a twist: all ten are healed, but the narrative turns on the one who comes back, and Luke delays the key detail to the end of verse 16 (he was a Samaritan). Verses 20 to 37 are a short discourse on the end, moving from a question by the Pharisees to teaching for the disciples. It is built on comparisons (lightning, Noah, Lot, Lot's wife) and pairs (two in a bed, two women grinding) that stress suddenness and separation. The phrase “your faith has made you well” uses a verb that can also mean saved, and Luke seems to mean both: the Samaritan receives more than clean skin. Verse 36 is missing from the earliest manuscripts and was likely added from Matthew 24:40.

outline.t: Unworthy servants who have only done their duty
Ten lepers healed; one Samaritan returns
The kingdom of God is in your midst
The day of the Son of Man, as in the days of Noah and Lot
Readiness and separation on that day

doctrines.note: Jesus ties forgiveness to repentance and removes any limit on it: seven times in a day. Rebuke and forgiveness belong together in the community of disciples, as honest confrontation and generous restoration.

The kingdom does not come with observable signs that can be tracked; it is already present in Jesus. Yet the day of the Son of Man still lies ahead and will come suddenly. The chapter holds together a kingdom present now and a kingdom yet to be completed.

The apostles ask for more faith; Jesus answers that the size of faith is not the issue, since even a mustard seed's worth is enough. What matters is faith's object, the God who acts. The Samaritan shows faith that returns in gratitude.

words.note: Entos, inside or within. In verse 21 the kingdom is entos you, which older translations rendered within you, suggesting an inward spiritual reality. Many modern translators prefer among you or in your midst, since Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and pointing to his own presence. Both readings are possible grammatically; the context favors the kingdom present in Jesus among them.

Eucharisteō, to give thanks. The Samaritan falls at Jesus' feet giving thanks, and gratitude is the mark that separates him from the nine. The same word later names the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist, the church's great thanksgiving.

Allogenēs, foreigner, literally one of another race. It appears only here in the New Testament. The same word was used on the inscriptions in Herod's temple that warned foreigners not to pass beyond the barrier into the inner courts. Jesus names the Samaritan a foreigner and praises him as the only one who returned to give glory to God.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus doing what only God can do and receiving what belongs to God. The Samaritan returns praising God and falls at Jesus' feet, and Jesus treats his return to him as giving glory to God. Jesus also names himself the Son of Man, a title drawn from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive everlasting dominion. Yet in verse 25 he insists that first the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. Glory comes by way of the cross. The healing of an outsider also anticipates the widening of the mission to Samaria and the nations in Acts.

hard.q: What does it mean that one will be taken and the other left, and is this about a rapture?
hard.a: The sayings in verses 34 and 35 picture sudden separation at the Son of Man's coming. Readers disagree on which one is fortunate. Some, especially in dispensational teaching, read taken as believers gathered to Christ and connect the verses to a rapture. Others note that in the examples just given, judgment is what overtakes people suddenly while Noah and Lot are spared, and the disciples' question, Where, Lord?, is answered with an image of vultures gathering over a carcass, which suggests judgment. On either reading, Jesus' point is the same: the day will come without warning, it will divide people who seemed to share the same life, and readiness cannot be borrowed from the person beside you. How these sayings fit a wider timeline of the end is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ.

questions: Jesus commands forgiveness seven times in a day. Where is repeated forgiveness hardest for you, and what does his command assume about the one forgiving?
Nine were healed and did not come back. What blessings have you received that you have never returned to thank God for?
The people of Noah's and Lot's day were eating, marrying, and building. How can ordinary, good things absorb us so fully that we stop watching?
